final_proof:
**Conventions.** A topological space $M$ is *locally Euclidean of dimension $d$* if every point $x\in M$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq M$ that is homeomorphic (with the subspace topology) to an open subset $V$ of $\R^d$ (Euclidean metric topology). A *local basis* of $m$ is a family $\mathcal B$ of open sets of $M$ each containing $m$ such that every open set $W\ni m$ contains some member of $\mathcal B$. Write $B(p,s)=\{y\in\R^d: \|y-p\|<s\}$. (For $d=0$, $\R^0=\{0\}$ and every open ball is $\{0\}$; the argument below covers this case verbatim.)

**Proof.** Since $M$ is locally Euclidean of dimension $d$, there are an open set $U\subseteq M$ with $m\in U$, an open set $V\subseteq\R^d$ and a homeomorphism $\phi:U\to V$. Put $p=\phi(m)\in V$. Since $V$ is open in $\R^d$, there is $r>0$ with $B(p,r)\subseteq V$. For $n\in\N$ define
$$s_n=\frac{r}{n+1},\qquad B_n=B(p,s_n)\subseteq V,\qquad U_n=\phi^{-1}(B_n)\subseteq U .$$

*Step 1: each $U_n$ is open in $M$ and contains $m$.* $B_n$ is open in $\R^d$ and contained in $V$, so $B_n=B_n\cap V$ is open in $V$. As $\phi$ is continuous, $U_n=\phi^{-1}(B_n)$ is open in $U$, i.e. $U_n=O\cap U$ for some open $O\subseteq M$; since $U$ is open in $M$, $U_n$ is open in $M$. Also $\phi(m)=p\in B_n$, so $m\in U_n$.

*Step 2: each $U_n$ is a homeomorphic image of an open ball of $\R^d$.* Since $\phi$ is a bijection $U\to V$, $\phi^{-1}:V\to U$ is a homeomorphism and maps $B_n$ bijectively onto $\phi^{-1}(B_n)=U_n$. The restriction of a continuous map to a subspace is continuous (and remains continuous when the codomain is shrunk to a subspace containing the image), so $\psi_n:=\phi^{-1}|_{B_n}:B_n\to U_n$ is a continuous bijection whose inverse $\phi|_{U_n}:U_n\to B_n$ is likewise continuous. Hence $\psi_n$ is a homeomorphism from the open ball $B_n$ onto $U_n$. (The subspace topology on $U_n$ induced from $U$ coincides with that induced from $M$, since $U$ carries the subspace topology from $M$.)

*Step 3: $\{U_n\}_{n\in\N}$ is a local basis at $m$.* Let $W\subseteq M$ be open with $m\in W$. Then $W\cap U$ is open in $U$ and contains $m$. Because $\phi:U\to V$ is a homeomorphism, it maps open subsets of $U$ to open subsets of $V$ (indeed $\phi(W\cap U)=(\phi^{-1})^{-1}(W\cap U)$ and $\phi^{-1}$ is continuous). So $\phi(W\cap U)$ is open in $V$, i.e. equals $G\cap V$ for some open $G\subseteq\R^d$; as $V$ is open in $\R^d$, $\phi(W\cap U)$ is open in $\R^d$. It contains $p=\phi(m)$, so there exists $\varepsilon>0$ with $B(p,\varepsilon)\subseteq\phi(W\cap U)$. By the Archimedean property choose $n\in\N$ with $n+1> r/\varepsilon$, so $s_n<\varepsilon$ and $B_n\subseteq B(p,\varepsilon)\subseteq \phi(W\cap U)$. Then, using that $\phi$ is a bijection onto $V$,
$$U_n=\phi^{-1}(B_n)\subseteq\phi^{-1}\big(\phi(W\cap U)\big)=W\cap U\subseteq W.$$

*Conclusion.* The family $\{U_n\}_{n\in\N}$ is indexed by $\N$, hence countable; by Step 1 its members are open neighbourhoods of $m$, by Step 3 it is a local basis of $m$, and by Step 2 each $U_n$ is the homeomorphic image of the open ball $B(p, r/(n+1))$ of $\R^d$. $\blacksquare$
